Question Choices: To solve f(x)=g(x) by graphing what feature should be located?
Hints: At a solution both functions have the same output.|Shared points satisfy both equations.
Solution: Locate every intersection of y=f(x) and y=g(x), then read its x-coordinate. At a shared point the two outputs agree. The x-coordinates solve f(x)=g(x); the full ordered pairs solve the two-equation system.

Question Choices: If y=2x+1 and y=7 intersect what is the x-coordinate of the solution?
Solution: Set the common outputs equal: 2x+(1)=7. Subtract 1 to get 2x=6, then divide by 2: x=3. The shared point is (3,7); substituting verifies both rules.

Question Choices: How many real solutions are shown when the graphs of two real functions y=f(x) and y=g(x) intersect at three points?
Hints: Each intersection gives one solution.|Count the shared points.
Solution: A solution is a shared ordered pair on the graphs. The stated number of intersections is 3, hence there are 3 real solutions. For two functions y=f(x),y=g(x), each intersection gives one distinct input solving f(x)=g(x).

Question Choices: If the graph of h(x)=f(x)-g(x) crosses the x-axis at x=4 what equation is solved there?
Solution: At the x-intercept h(4)=0. Since h=f-g, f(4)-g(4)=0, so f(4)=g(4). Thus x=4 solves f(x)=g(x). Touching the axis would also give equality; crossing is not required.

Question Choices: A graphing calculator shows an intersection near x=2.347. Rounded to the nearest tenth what is x?
Hints: Look at the hundredths digit.|The hundredths digit is 4.
Solution: In 2.347 the tenths digit is 3 and the next digit, the hundredths digit, is 4. Since 4<5, retain 3 and drop later digits: 2.3. It is 0.047 from 2.3 and 0.053 from 2.4, confirming the nearer tenth.

Question Choices: Why should the viewing window be chosen carefully when solving by graphing?
Question Answers: an intersection can be hidden outside the window|the window may hide solutions|to see all relevant intersections
Hints: The display only shows a selected range.|Solutions outside that range are invisible.
Solution: A viewing window displays only selected input and output ranges. An intersection outside either range is invisible. Expand and adjust the window, then use algebra or known graph behavior to check completeness; a screen alone does not prove no other solutions exist.

Question Choices: A word problem compares cost C(x) and revenue R(x). What does an intersection represent?
Question Answers: break-even point|equal cost and revenue|break even
Hints: At an intersection the outputs are equal.|Profit is zero when revenue equals cost.
Solution: At an intersection C(x)=R(x), so profit R(x)-C(x)=0. It is a break-even point if the input lies in the model's meaningful domain, such as a nonnegative production quantity.

Question Choices: If two equations have exactly the same graph, a curve containing infinitely many points, how many solutions does their system have?
Hints: Every point on one curve is on the other.|The equations are equivalent.
Solution: When both graphs are exactly the same curve containing infinitely many points, every point on it satisfies both equations. Thus there are infinitely many ordered-pair solutions.

Question Choices: If two horizontal lines are distinct how many solutions does their system have?
Hints: Distinct parallel lines never meet.|No intersection means no solution.
Solution: Distinct horizontal lines have different fixed y-values. No ordered pair can have both values, so the parallel lines never intersect and the system has no solution.

Question Choices: Solve x^2=9 by graphing y=x^2 and y=9. Enter the x-values in increasing order.
Hints: Find where the parabola reaches height 9.|The intersections are symmetric.
Solution: Substitute y=9: x^2-0=9, so x^2=9. Both square roots work, x=-3 and x=3. Each produces y=9 in the original curve. Enter the negative x-value first.
